title: Efficient Ion-Photon Quantum Interface with Long-Working-Distance Exceeding 26 mm
authors: Jungwoo Choi, Inhyuk Oh, Chanyang Im, Gibeom Son, Junki Kim
abstract: Trapped-ion quantum networks rely on efficient ion-photon interfaces, while objective-based free-space collection systems must balance high photon collection with sufficient working distance for practical integration with ion-trap hardware. Here, we design and characterize an ion-photon interface with a long working distance of 26.15 mm and a high numerical aperture of 0.5. The core of the interface is a photon-collection objective consisting of six commercial spherical lenses with optimized spacing. The interface achieved an overall fiber-coupled photon-detection efficiency of (1.29$\pm$0.09)% from the ion to the detector and maintains fiber coupling over several hours without active realignment, supporting stable operation of the ion-to-fiber interface. Photon-correlation measurements show clear antibunching in the fiber-coupled fluorescence, confirming the preservation of non-classical photon statistics. These results demonstrate a practical implementation of a long-working-distance photon collection interface for trapped-ion quantum network experiments.
summary: This paper presents the design and characterization of a novel, high-performance ion-photon interface capable of operating over a long working distance (26.15 mm). By optimizing a custom objective lens system, the authors achieved a stable, fiber-coupled detection efficiency of $\approx 1.3\%$ for trapped-ion fluorescence. This practical implementation is crucial for scaling up trapped-ion quantum network experiments.
main_problem: The primary challenge was designing an efficient ion-photon quantum interface that could maintain high photon collection efficiency while providing a long working distance for practical integration with existing ion-trap hardware.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated an interface with a working distance of 26.15 mm and an overall fiber-coupled detection efficiency of $(1.29 \pm 0.09)\%$, while confirming non-classical photon statistics via antibunching measurements.
method: The interface was constructed using a custom objective lens system of six spherical lenses, which was characterized by optimizing lens spacing and performing detailed photon-correlation measurements.
model_or_system: The experiment utilizes trapped $^{138}	ext{Ba}^+$ ions in a 4-rod Paul trap. The system involves collecting fluorescence photons emitted from the ion, which are then coupled into a Single-Mode Fiber (SMF).
key_observables: Overall fiber-coupled photon-detection efficiency ($\approx 1.3\%$), antibunching ($g^{(2)}(0) = 0.042$), and signal stability over several hours.
important_parameters: Working Distance (WD) > 26 mm, Numerical Aperture (NA) = 0.5, and the use of a six-lens objective assembly.
main_assumptions: The analysis notes that initial simulations overestimated the coupling efficiency, and the final measurements were limited by the practical assembly of the complex optical system.
figures_summary: Figures show the schematic cross-section of the objective lens system (Fig. 1), optimized through-focus images across an axial scan (Fig. 2), and the mechanical integration setup and stability monitoring (Fig. 4).
paper_structure: The paper details the design of the long-working-distance objective, presents the experimental setup integrated with the ion trap, characterizes the optical performance (efficiency and stability), and confirms the quantum nature of the emitted light via correlation measurements.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major engineering bottleneck in trapped-ion quantum networking: coupling high-quality quantum light sources to external fiber infrastructure while maintaining operational stability and spatial constraints.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Schematic cross-section of the long-WD objective lens system. The working distance of the custom objective is 26.15 mm, defined as the mechanical clearance from the ion position to the assembled objective housing. The gray region marks the vacuum-chamber interior, which houses a four-rod Paul trap that confines the ions (camera image: 17 138Ba+ ions). Black solid lines indicate the marginal rays that define the object-space NA of 0.5. At the focal plane, the full marginal-ray bundle falls within the Airy disk (right inset), as required for the diffraction-limited design. The final cylindrical lens (Thorlabs LJ1516RM-A) is used in the experiment to correct residual astigmatism.

Fig. 2 Through-focus fluorescence imaging and ray-tracing simulations of a single 138Ba+ ion. Experimental images after alignment optimization are shown in the top row, and corresponding ray- tracing simulations are shown in the bottom row. Images were acquired at 100 µm axial steps from −300 µm to +300 µm relative to the focal plane. Scale bar: 10 µm.

Fig. 3 Intensity profile characterization by scanning the single-mode fiber tip. (a) Normalized pho- ton count rate over a 20 µm × 20 µm area (1 µm steps). (b) Cross-sections along X and Z axes. Experimental data and Gaussian fits (blue markers and blue dashed curves) are compared with the convolution of the simulated PSF and the fiber mode profile (black solid curves).

Fig. 4 Mechanical integration and passive mechanical stability. (a) Computer-aided design (CAD) model of the custom chamber base and objective mount. (b) Photograph of the experimental appa- ratus. (c) Normalized fiber-coupled fluorescence monitored for 4 h without realignment, showing the signal remains above 80% of its initial value for 58 min and reaches 60% at 231 min.

Fig. 5 Second-order correlation function g(2)(τ) of single-ion fluorescence coupled to a SMF. Gray dots represent the experimental data, and the black solid line indicates the theoretical fit based on the 3-level optical Bloch equations.
